figureFiles.caption: The same eight decisions before and after writing a spec. In the one-line request every decision falls to a model default; in the spec seven are made by you and one is delegated on purpose, with limits and a request to report the choice.
The six parts of a spec, filled in for Lamplighter v0.1, with the failure each part prevents. Try covering one row and imagining what the model would do without it.

Every result is checked against the acceptance criteria before anything is revised. A failing check leads to a scoped revision and a fresh check of every criterion; passing leads back to the spec, which stays the record of what you want.

lesson.hook: On September 23, 1999, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter as it fired its engine to enter orbit around Mars. The investigation found that a ground software file called “Small Forces” had reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds, while the document both teams worked from, the Software Interface Specification, required newton-seconds. Every firing’s effect was underestimated by a factor of 4.45, and the spacecraft’s path had drifted far lower than the navigators believed. The specification named the right unit. What failed was the check: nothing in the process compared the delivered file against the spec before it was trusted. Every time you ask an AI for something, you are writing an interface specification for a contractor who works in seconds and rarely asks questions. This chapter is about writing it so that both of you can tell when it has been met.
lesson.overview: This chapter is the foundation for the rest of the book. Section 1.1 explains why vague requests come back competent but generic: models fill every unmade decision with a default and quietly pick one reading of ambiguous words. Section 1.2 introduces the six-part spec (goal, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, examples, output format) and the requirements engineering standards behind it. Section 1.3 shows how to turn qualities like “readable” and “feels good” into checks, and how examples teach format and style. Section 1.4 covers asking for output you can use and writing a revision that changes only what you name. Along the way you write the first spec for Lamplighter, the small browser platformer you will build across all twelve chapters, and every idea comes with a before and after prompt.
objectives: Identify underspecified and ambiguous parts of a request and predict the defaults a model will choose for them.
Write a six-part spec with goal, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, examples and output format.
Translate qualities such as “readable” or “feels good” into measurable criteria and Given/When/Then scenarios.
Request an output format you can use directly, including an assumption list or clarifying questions where they pay off.
Write a scoped revision request that names a failing criterion and protects everything else from regressions.

sections.title: Why vague prompts fail
reading: Ask a coding agent to “make a cozy platformer about a lamplighter” and you will get a game. It will probably be a single web page with a rectangle for a hero, arrow keys to move, a jump, some floating platforms and perhaps warm orange colors standing in for “cozy.” It will not be the game you pictured, because almost nothing you pictured was in the request. Your sentence left most decisions open: where the game runs, which keys do what, how big the level is, what winning means, what “cozy” looks and sounds like. That condition is called **underspecification**: the request fits many different outputs, and the words do not choose among them. A model does not leave those decisions blank. It fills each one with a **default**, roughly the most typical choice for requests like yours (Chapter 2 explains why), and that is why underspecified prompts tend to come back competent and average (Figure 1.1).

Anthropic’s guide to prompting its Claude models puts the problem in human terms. It asks you to think of the model as “a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows,” and says that the more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result [1]. Its test for a prompt, which it calls the golden rule, is to show the prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it; if they would be confused, the model will be too [1]. The comparison puts the blame in the right place. A new hire who builds the wrong thing from a one-line brief is not stupid. The brief was missing everything that lived only in the manager’s head.

Underspecification has a cousin, **ambiguity**, where the words are present but can be read more than one way. “Make the lamps lighter” could mean brighter, paler, smaller on disk or lower in weight in the physics code. “Fix the button” assumes the model knows which button and what is wrong with it. “Make the enemies faster” leaves open movement, attack rate or spawn rate, and in which levels. Models are poor at catching this. Alisa Liu and colleagues built AmbiEnt, a set of 1,645 linguist-annotated examples of ambiguous sentences, and asked models to spell out the possible readings; crowdworkers judged GPT-4’s disambiguations correct only 32% of the time, against 90% for the ones written for the dataset [2]. Handed an ambiguous instruction, a model usually picks one reading and carries on without telling you it chose.

People new to prompting leave these gaps for understandable reasons. J. D. Zamfirescu-Pereira and colleagues watched people without AI training design prompts for a chatbot. Their participants tried ideas opportunistically rather than systematically, overgeneralized from a single success or failure, and carried over habits from giving instructions to other people [3]. With a human colleague, shared context fills the holes: they were in yesterday’s meeting, and they know your taste. A model knows only what is in the conversation in front of it, plus general patterns from its training. Your taste, your project and your earlier decisions exist for it only if they are written down where it can read them.

Small differences in wording and layout can also move results more than you would guess. Melanie Sclar and colleagues changed only the formatting of prompts, such as separators, spacing and capitalization, while keeping their meaning the same. On one open model, LLaMA-2-13B, accuracy on few-shot tasks varied by up to 76 percentage points across formats, and the sensitivity did not disappear with larger models, more examples or instruction tuning [4]. Their tasks were benchmarks, not creative briefs, but two habits follow for any prompt. Do not assume the model understood you because it understood a similar prompt last week, and do not judge a prompt by a single run.

The cure is not a longer prompt but fewer unmade decisions. Before you send a request, list the questions a capable stranger would need answered, then answer each one or hand it over on purpose. Handing it over on purpose, **explicit delegation**, sounds like this: “Choose the platform layout yourself, keep every lamp reachable, and list the choices you made.” Delegating is often the right call, since the model may know conventions you do not. Silent delegation is the problem, because you discover the decision only after it has been built into the result.

keyTerms.def: A request that fits many different outputs because it leaves decisions unstated.
The choice a model makes for a decision the request left open, usually the most typical choice for similar requests.
Wording that can reasonably be read in more than one way, such as “lighter” meaning brighter, paler or smaller.
Anthropic’s check that a prompt a colleague with little context could not follow will also confuse the model.
Handing a decision to the model on purpose, with limits, and asking it to report what it chose.

example.title: Worked example: auditing Lamplighter’s first request
steps: Before: “Make a cozy platformer about a lamplighter.” Read it as a stranger would, and write down every question you would need answered before starting.

The questions: Where does it run? In which language? Which keys? How big is the level? How do you win or lose? What does “cozy” mean in color, sound and pace? Placeholder art or finished sprites? What should come back: files, an explanation, both?
Mark each question. “Cozy” is ambiguous (a word with several readings); the other seven are underspecified (nothing was said). Eight decisions, none made.

Decide or delegate each one: the browser, plain JavaScript, arrow keys and Space, one screen-sized level, five lamps to light before a 90-second timer runs out, colored rectangles for art. Delegate the platform layout explicitly.

After: “Make a first playable build of a 2D platformer called Lamplighter that runs by opening index.html in Chrome. Plain JavaScript and HTML canvas, 960×540, no libraries. Arrow keys move, Space jumps, E lights a lamp the player is touching. One level with five lamps; light all five before a 90-second timer ends to win; if the timer ends, show ‘Night fell’ and restart with R. Colored rectangles for all art. You choose the platform layout; keep every lamp reachable and list the layout choices you made.”
example.takeaway: Every question a stranger would ask is a decision; answer it or delegate it out loud, so nothing gets decided silently.

misconception.myth: A smart enough model will figure out what I mean.
misconception.fact: Capability helps a model carry out a request, not recover the parts you left out. The model has your words and its general training, so every missing decision gets a typical default. Anthropic’s own guidance tells users to be explicit, and in the AmbiEnt study even GPT-4 usually failed to spell out the readings of an ambiguous sentence correctly.

practice.q: A reader asks an AI to “make the title screen pop more.” What is the main problem with this request?
choices: It is too short for the model to process
“Pop” has several possible readings and no result is defined, so the model will choose its own
It does not begin with a role such as “You are a designer”
It needs to be written in capital letters for emphasis
practice.explanation: “Pop” is ambiguous (more contrast, motion, bigger type, brighter color?) and nothing says what a finished result looks like, so the model fills both gaps with defaults. Length is not the issue, a role would not resolve the ambiguity, and capitals add emphasis but no information.

practice.q: You ask an image generator for “a lamplighter at night, nice lighting.” Name three decisions this request leaves to defaults, then rewrite it so that it settles two of them and delegates one explicitly.
practice.answer: Open decisions include framing (close-up or full figure), the light source and its color, the art style or medium, the setting, and the aspect ratio. A rewrite: “A full-body view of an old lamplighter on a rooftop at dusk, lit only by the warm lamp he has just lit, with a cool blue sky behind him, in a soft painted style, 16:9. Choose his pose yourself and tell me which pose you chose.”
practice.explanation: A good answer names concrete open decisions (not just “details”), settles at least two with specific words, and hands one over with a request to report the choice. Chapter 7 gives the exact vocabulary for framing and light.

practice.q: While building a level, a coding agent also added a settings menu you never asked for. Which change to your original request would most directly have prevented this?
choices: Adding “please” and “thank you”
Saying what is out of scope (“no menus in this build”) and asking it to list anything it adds beyond the request
Asking for the code in a different programming language
Sending the same request again
practice.explanation: The menu was an unmade decision the agent settled on its own. Stating the scope makes the decision for it, and asking for a list of additions surfaces any remaining silent choices. Politeness, language choice and resending do not touch the gap.

sections.title: The anatomy of a spec
reading: A **spec**, short for specification, is a description of something to be built, written so that one person can build it and another can check it. Requirements engineers have worked for decades on what makes such descriptions succeed. Their international standard, ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, lists characteristics that each individual requirement should have, among them that it be necessary, unambiguous, complete, singular (one requirement per statement), feasible and **verifiable** [1]. Two of these do most of the work in prompts. Unambiguous means only one reasonable reading. Verifiable means there is a way to show the requirement has been met. A prompt is a spec for a very fast contractor who starts work the moment you press Enter, so the same standards apply.

The hook of this chapter shows what a spec can and cannot do. The Mars Climate Orbiter’s Software Interface Specification defined the format and units of a file passed from ground software to the navigation team, and it called for thruster impulse in newton-seconds. The ground software file named “Small Forces” reported pound-force seconds instead, so the navigation software underestimated the effect of thruster firings by a factor of 4.45 [2]. Among the contributing causes, the investigation board listed the lack of complete end-to-end verification of the navigation software and related models [2]. The spec was right. It failed because nothing checked the delivered file against it, which is why every spec in this book ends with criteria you can check.

This book uses six parts for every spec (Figure 1.2). The **goal** says what you want and why. The **context** says who it is for, where it will run and what already exists. The **constraints** set the limits. The acceptance criteria say how you will know it is done. The examples show what good looks like. The output format says what shape the answer should take. Each part prevents a particular failure. Without a goal the model works hard on the wrong thing; without context it guesses the platform and audience; without constraints it picks tools and scope for you; without criteria neither of you can tell when to stop; without examples it guesses the style; without a format you get prose when you needed files. Sections 1.3 and 1.4 cover the last three.

The goal is the part people skip most often, because it feels obvious to them. Anthropic’s documentation recommends giving the reason behind an instruction, not just the instruction. Its example replaces “NEVER use ellipses” with an explanation that the response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine that cannot pronounce them, and it notes that the model can generalize from the explanation [3]. A goal with a reason works the same way: “a first playable build, to test whether jumping and lighting lamps is fun before I spend time on art” tells the model to put its effort into controls and none into graphics. Context covers the rest of what lives in your head: your skill level, your machine, your files, your audience. The same guide suggests placing long documents near the top of a prompt, above the instructions, and wrapping each kind of content in its own labeled XML tag so instructions, context and examples are not confused [3].

A **constraint** is a limit the output must respect. Hard constraints are requirements (“plain JavaScript, no libraries, exactly two files”); soft constraints are preferences the model may trade off (“prefer short functions”). Say which is which. A useful special case is the **non-goal**, a statement of what is out of scope: “no menus, sound or touch controls in this build.” A model that has not been told the scope may reasonably add a feature or tidy a file nobody asked about, and a non-goal draws the line before it is crossed. Where you can, phrase limits as what to do instead of what to avoid. Anthropic’s guide suggests replacing “Do not use markdown in your response” with “Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs” [3].

A spec should be as long as the decisions you need to fix, and no longer. A one-off image may need two sentences; a feature a coding agent will work on for an hour deserves a page. Adjectives such as “amazing,” “polished” or “AAA quality” add length without adding a decision, because nobody can check them. The standard’s rule that each requirement be singular helps here: one statement, one requirement, so each can pass or fail on its own and a reviewer can point at the one that failed [1]. Write the six parts, run the golden rule test from Section 1.1, then send.

keyTerms.def: A description of something to be built, precise enough that one person can build it and another can check it.
The outcome you want and the reason you want it, which tells the model where to spend effort.
The facts the model cannot know on its own: audience, platform, skill level, existing files and decisions already made.
A limit the output must respect; hard constraints are requirements, soft constraints are preferences that may be traded off.
An explicit statement of what is out of scope for this request, such as “no sound in this build.”
Stated so that there is a practical way to show whether the requirement has been met.

example.title: Worked example: Lamplighter spec v0.1, part by part
steps: Goal: “A first playable build of Lamplighter, to test whether climbing and lighting lamps is fun before any art or sound is made.”
Context: “I am not a programmer. I will run the game by opening index.html in Chrome on a laptop. Nothing exists yet; these are the project’s first files.”

Constraints: “Hard: plain JavaScript and HTML canvas, no libraries, no build step, two files (index.html and game.js), canvas 960×540. Soft: keep functions short and commented. Non-goals: no menus, sound, saving or touch controls.”
Acceptance criteria and example: the checks written in Section 1.3, plus a text sketch of the level, a few rows of characters in which # is roof, L is a lamp and P is the player’s start.
Output format: “Reply with both complete files, then a bulleted list of every choice you made that this spec did not settle.”
example.takeaway: Each part of the spec closes one door the model would otherwise open on its own.

misconception.myth: A longer prompt is always a better prompt.
misconception.fact: Length helps only when it carries decisions. Adjectives like “polished” or “stunning” cannot be checked and give the model nothing new, and repeating an instruction in capitals is no substitute for the reason behind it. A short prompt that settles the six parts beats a long one that circles them.

practice.q: In a spec, which part is “No sound or menus in this build”?
choices: Goal
Context
Non-goal, a kind of constraint
Output format
practice.explanation: It marks what is out of scope, which is a non-goal. It does not say what you want or why (goal), describe your situation (context), or say what shape the answer should take (output format).

practice.q: You want an AI to write button labels for Lamplighter’s menu. Which request best follows Anthropic’s advice to give the reason behind an instruction?
choices: “SHORT LABELS ONLY!!!”
“Labels must fit buttons 120 px wide at 16 px type, about 12 characters, because the menu has to fit small laptop screens.”
“You are the world’s best UX writer.”
“Write labels. Do not write long labels. Do not write long labels.”
practice.explanation: The second choice states a checkable limit and the reason for it, so the model can generalize (for example, preferring short verbs). Capitals and repetition add emphasis without information, and a flattering role sets no limit at all.

practice.q: Write a goal with its reason, two hard constraints and one non-goal for this request: “Make a loading screen for Lamplighter.”
practice.answer: Goal: “A loading screen that shows while level assets load, so players are not left looking at a blank canvas.” Hard constraints: “Draw it on the existing 960×540 canvas in game.js with no new libraries; it must disappear as soon as loading finishes.” Non-goal: “No tips, animations or music on this screen yet.”
practice.explanation: A strong answer gives a goal that includes why, constraints that are checkable and genuinely limiting (technology, size, behavior), and a non-goal that names something a model might plausibly add on its own.

sections.title: Acceptance criteria and examples
reading: An **acceptance criterion** is a condition the result must meet to count as done, written so that anyone who checks it gets the same answer. Software teams attach a short list of them to each piece of work, and they are the verifiable requirements of Section 1.2 in practical form. Anthropic’s guide to evaluating prompts makes the point with a contrast: “The model should classify sentiments well” is a bad criterion, while an F1 score of at least 0.85 on a held-out test set of 10,000 posts is a good one, because it is specific and measurable [1]. A game or an app rarely needs statistics, but it always needs the same move: replace a quality you can only feel with a check you can run.

Most vague words in prompts can be translated. “Fast” becomes “the level appears less than two seconds after the page opens on my laptop.” “Readable” becomes a number. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, the W3C’s accessibility standard, are written almost entirely as criteria of this kind; success criterion 1.4.3 requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 between normal text and its background, and 3:1 for large text [2]. “Make the HUD text readable” leaves the model guessing, while “HUD text meets the WCAG 2.2 contrast minimum of 4.5:1” can be checked with any contrast tool. When a quality resists numbers, as “cozy” does, list features you could observe: four named colors, music no faster than 90 beats per minute, no sudden loud sounds.

For behavior, one format works especially well. Behaviour-driven development, the practice built into the Cucumber testing tool and its Gherkin language, writes each scenario in three clauses: Given a starting situation, When something happens, Then an expected outcome follows [3]. “Given the player is touching an unlit lamp, when they press E, then the lamp lights and the lamp counter goes up by one.” Each **Given/When/Then scenario** is one check, it reads as plain English, and a coding agent can turn it into an automated test (Chapter 4). Writing three or four of them also pushes you to think about **edge cases**, the unusual situations where bugs hide: pressing E in mid-air, at a lamp that is already lit, or at the instant the timer reaches zero.

Criteria say what must be true; examples show what good looks like. Putting a few worked examples in the prompt is called **few-shot prompting** (with one example, one-shot). Anthropic calls examples “one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude’s output format, tone, and structure,” and recommends three to five that are relevant to the real task, diverse enough to cover edge cases, and wrapped in example tags so the model can tell them apart from the instructions [4]. Diversity matters because a model copies more than you intend. If all three level sketches you provide are wide and flat, expect a wide, flat fourth.

Research on why examples work supports that caution. Sewon Min and colleagues tested demonstrations on classification tasks across 12 models and found that replacing the correct answers in the examples with random ones lowered performance only slightly; what the examples mainly conveyed was the set of possible answers, the kind of input text and the overall format [5]. For a vibe coder the lesson is practical. Examples are strongest at teaching shape: format, length, tone and structure. They also teach their accidents along with their intent, so vary everything you do not want copied, and if you include a **counterexample** of what you do not want, label it plainly as one.

Criteria and examples work best together. A criterion such as “each lamp description is one sentence of 15 to 25 words” can be checked but says nothing about voice; an example sets the voice but cannot say which of its features are required. Give both, and say which features of the examples are requirements and which are incidental. For Lamplighter, each lamp shows a one-line note when it is lit. The spec gives the criterion (one sentence, 15 to 25 words, present tense, no exclamation marks), three example notes in different moods, and a line saying that the examples set the voice but their subjects (a baker, a cat, a train) should not be repeated.

keyTerms.def: A condition the result must meet to count as done, stated so that anyone checking it gets the same pass or fail.
A behavior check written as a starting situation, an action and an expected outcome, from behaviour-driven development.
An unusual or boundary situation, such as an input at the exact moment a timer ends, where failures tend to hide.
Including a small number of worked examples in a prompt to show the model the format, tone and structure you want.
An example of what you do not want, clearly labeled so the model does not copy it.

example.title: Worked example: from “the jump should feel good” to checks
steps: Before: “Make the jump feel good.” Ask what you would actually see or measure in a jump you like. Play a platformer you enjoy and watch the jump closely.

Turn what you see into numbers you can tune: “A full jump rises about 3 tiles (96 px with 32 px tiles). Tapping Space gives a shorter jump than holding it. The player reaches the top of a full jump in roughly 0.4 s.” These are your design targets, not universal truths, and Chapter 10 shows how designers tune them.

Add scenarios for edge cases: “Given the player walked off a roof edge less than 0.1 s ago, when they press Space, then they still jump.” “Given the player is in mid-air, when they press Space, then nothing happens.”
Add one example in words: describe the jump of a game you like in your own terms (quick rise, short hang at the top, faster fall) instead of only naming the game.
After: the request now has three numeric targets, two scenarios and one described reference. Each one can pass or fail the first time you play the build.
example.takeaway: “Feels good” becomes buildable when you write down what you would observe if it did.

misconception.myth: Acceptance criteria are paperwork for big companies, not something you need for a quick AI prompt.
misconception.fact: They matter more with AI, not less. A model produces a finished-looking result in seconds and will not tell you which of your unstated hopes it missed. Three or four checks take a minute to write and turn review from a vague impression into a list you can tick off.

practice.q: Which of these is an acceptance criterion?
choices: The pause menu should look professional
Pressing Esc during play opens the pause menu, and pressing Esc again closes it
Use your best judgment on the pause menu
The pause menu should be intuitive
practice.explanation: Only the second can be checked with a clear pass or fail. “Professional” and “intuitive” are qualities without a test, and “use your best judgment” is delegation, not a criterion.

practice.q: Write two Given/When/Then scenarios for this Lamplighter feature: the player falls off the bottom of the screen.
practice.answer: “Given the player is falling below the bottom edge of the canvas, when their box is fully off screen, then they reappear at the last lamp they lit (or at the start if none) and the timer keeps running.” “Given the player falls off screen at the moment the timer reaches zero, when the frame updates, then the ‘Night fell’ message shows and the player does not respawn.”
practice.explanation: Good scenarios name a precise starting state, a single triggering event and an observable outcome. The second scenario targets an edge case where two rules (respawn and time-out) could conflict.

practice.q: You give an AI three example lamp descriptions. All are exactly two sentences long and all mention brass. You ask for ten more. What is the likely result?
choices: The model will ignore the length and the brass, since only instructions count
The model will tend to copy the two-sentence length and the brass detail, so vary them unless they are requirements
The model will refuse because the examples are too similar
The examples will only work if each is labeled correct or incorrect
practice.explanation: Examples teach shape and surface features, as Min and colleagues found for format. Features shared by every example are likely to be copied. Vary what is incidental, or state which features are required.

sections.title: Output format and the first revision
reading: The **output format** is the shape of what comes back: which files, in which language, with what structure, at what length, in what markup. It is the most practical part of a spec, because it decides how much work you do after the model finishes. Ask for the form you will use. If you will paste code into files, ask for complete files with their names, not fragments. If you will compare options, ask for a table with the columns you need. Anthropic’s guide advises being specific about the desired format, telling the model what to do rather than what not to do, and matching the style of your prompt to the style you want back, since the formatting of a prompt can influence the formatting of the response [1].

When the output will be read by a program instead of a person, ask for **structured output**: data in a fixed, machine-readable shape, usually JSON (JavaScript Object Notation). For a Lamplighter level that might be an object with a width and height in tiles, a list of roofs as rectangles and a list of lamps with x and y positions. In a chat window, show the exact shape with a short template. Through an API, some vendors can enforce the shape. As of October 2026, Anthropic’s structured outputs feature constrains Claude’s responses to a **JSON schema** you supply, a description of which fields an object must have and what type each one is, so that the result can always be parsed [2].

Two format requests pay for themselves on any larger task. The first is an **assumption list**: “after the files, list every decision you made that this spec did not settle.” It turns the hidden defaults of Section 1.1 into a list you can read in a minute, and it shows you what to add to the spec next time. The second reverses the order of work: “before writing any code, ask me up to five questions about anything ambiguous, then wait for my answers.” **Clarifying questions** cost one extra message and catch ambiguity before it is built in. Use them when the task is large or a wrong guess is expensive, and skip them for cheap drafts where looking at a result is faster than answering questions.

No spec is perfect, so the first result starts a loop: build, check every acceptance criterion, revise (Figure 1.3). A good **revision request** names the failing criterion and the evidence, states the change, and fences off everything else: “Criterion 3 fails: a full jump rises about 6 tiles, not 3. Lower the jump to 3 tiles. Change only the jump constants in game.js and leave everything else as it is.” The fence matters. A model asked to fix one thing may change more than you wanted, and a change that breaks something that used to work is called a **regression** (Chapter 4). After each revision, recheck all the criteria, not only the one you fixed.

Change one thing per revision when you can, and do not draw conclusions from one run. The formatting study in Section 1.1 found large swings from small changes that kept the meaning the same [3], and the study of non-expert prompt designers found that newcomers often overgeneralized from a single success or failure [4]. If a result is good, write down what produced it; if it is bad, find the criterion it fails before you rewrite the prompt. A bare “that’s wrong, try again” gives the model no new information, so you are simply asking for another draw from the same request.

When you change your mind, change the spec too. Midway through a session it is tempting to steer only in chat (“actually make it four lamps”), but after a dozen such messages the real requirements are scattered across the conversation, and neither you nor the model can see them in one place. Keep the written spec as the single record of what you want and paste the current version when you start a new session. Chapter 12 builds a whole project on that habit, with a project binder that any AI tool can pick up.

keyTerms.def: The shape of the deliverable: files, language, structure, length and markup.
Output in a fixed, machine-readable shape, usually JSON, so a program can use it directly.
A description of the fields a JSON object must contain and the type of each, used to define or enforce structured output.
A requested list of every decision the model made that the spec did not settle.
A follow-up that names the failing criterion with evidence, the change to make, and what must stay the same.
A change that breaks something that previously worked.

example.title: Worked example: the first revision of Lamplighter v0.1
steps: Run the build and check every criterion. Lamps light when touched and E is pressed (pass). The timer and both end messages work (pass). A full jump rises about 6 tiles instead of 3 (fail). A lamp lights while the player stands about 64 px away (fail). The model also added a music on/off button, which the spec never asked for.
Before, the tempting revision: “The jump is wrong and some other stuff is off, fix it.” It names no criterion, gives no evidence and puts no fence around the rest of the code.
Name each failure with its evidence and target: jump height about 6 tiles, target 3 tiles (96 px); lamp lights at about 64 px, target only when the player’s box overlaps the lamp’s box.
Fence off the rest and deal with the extra: sound is a non-goal for v0.1, so the button goes.

After: “Two acceptance criteria fail. (1) A full jump rises about 6 tiles; it should rise 3 tiles (96 px). (2) Lamps light from about 64 px away; they should light only when the player’s box overlaps the lamp’s box. Also remove the music button, since sound is out of scope for v0.1. Change only what these fixes need, and list every line you changed.”
Rerun and recheck all criteria, not only the two that failed, to catch any regression.
example.takeaway: A revision request is a small spec: the failing check, the change, and a fence around everything else.

misconception.myth: If the answer is wrong, keep regenerating until it comes out right.
misconception.fact: Regenerating samples the same request again, so you may get a result that is wrong in a new way, and you learn nothing about why. Find the criterion that failed and say so. If no criterion failed and you are still unhappy, the spec was missing something you care about, so add it as a new criterion.

practice.q: Your game code will load Lamplighter’s level data from the AI’s answer. Which output format request fits best?
choices: “Describe the level in a few paragraphs.”
“Return only a JSON object with width and height in tiles, a roofs list (x, y, w, h) and a lamps list (x, y), and no other text.”
“Make a nice level and show it to me.”
“Write the level as a table in your favorite format.”
practice.explanation: A program needs a fixed, machine-readable shape. The second choice names the fields, the units and the absence of extra text. Prose descriptions and free-choice formats would have to be converted by hand.

practice.q: A coding agent fixed the jump, but now the player falls through one of the roofs, which worked before. Name what has happened and write the revision request.
practice.answer: It is a regression: the fix broke behavior that previously worked. Revision: “The jump fix caused a regression: the player now falls through the roof at the top right (about x 22, y 6 in tiles), which was solid in the previous build. Restore solid collision on every roof while keeping the new 3-tile jump. Change only collision or jump code, list the lines you changed, and confirm the five original criteria still pass.”
practice.explanation: A good answer uses the word regression, gives evidence (which roof, that it used to work), keeps the earlier fix, fences the change and asks for all criteria to be rechecked.

practice.q: When are clarifying questions from the model most worth the extra message?
choices: For a quick image draft you can regenerate in seconds
Before an agent starts a multi-file feature whose requirements contain several ambiguous points
When you have already given a complete spec with acceptance criteria and examples
Never, because questions always slow the work down
practice.explanation: Questions pay off when a wrong guess is expensive and ambiguity is present. For cheap drafts, looking at a result is faster; with a complete spec there is little left to ask; and “never” ignores the cost of building on a wrong reading.

interactives.title: Vague or exact?
interactives.intro: Sort each request. Ask yourself: could two different people check this and agree on whether it was done?
buckets: Vague: leaves the decision to the model

items.text: Make the menu pop.
items.why: “Pop” has no agreed meaning, so the model picks one reading silently.

items.text: The pause menu opens with Esc and closes with Esc or the Resume button.
items.why: Two observable behaviors, each of which passes or fails.

items.text: Give the game a cozy vibe.
items.why: “Cozy” needs observable features: named colors, a tempo, the pace of play.

items.text: Use only these four colors: #1B2A41, #F2A541, #F5E9D3, #5C4B51.
items.why: Anyone can check every pixel against four hex codes.

items.text: Make the enemies harder.
items.why: Harder how: faster, tougher, more of them, in which levels?

items.text: Bats fly 20% faster in level 2 than in level 1, and level 3 adds one more bat.
items.why: Specific quantities in specific places.

items.text: Clean up the code.
items.why: Which files, toward what standard, and what behavior must not change?

items.text: Split game.js into player.js, level.js and main.js without changing gameplay; all five acceptance checks must still pass.
items.why: A defined structure plus a test that guards against regressions.

items.text: A 16-bar music loop at 90 BPM that repeats with no audible gap.
items.why: Length, tempo and a loop condition you can hear and measure (Chapter 9).

items.text: Make it feel more professional.
items.why: No feature of “professional” is named, so nothing can be checked.

interactives.title: Which part of the spec is this?
interactives.intro: Each sentence comes from Lamplighter’s first spec. Sort it into one of the six parts. Notice which parts you had to think hardest about.

items.text: A first playable build, to test whether lighting lamps is fun before any art is made.
items.why: What is wanted and why.

items.text: I will run it by opening index.html in Chrome on a laptop.
items.why: A fact about your situation the model cannot know.

items.text: I am not a programmer, and this is the first file in the project.
items.why: Skill level and existing state are context.

items.text: Plain JavaScript and HTML canvas, no libraries, exactly two files.
items.why: Hard limits on how it may be built.

items.text: No menus or sound in this build.
items.why: A non-goal, the scope-setting kind of constraint.

items.text: Lighting all five lamps before the timer ends shows “Level complete.”
items.why: A condition you can check pass or fail.

items.text: Given the player touches an unlit lamp, when they press E, then the lamp lights.
items.why: A Given/When/Then scenario is an acceptance criterion for behavior.

items.text: Here is a level sketch in characters: # is roof, L is a lamp, P is the start.
items.why: It shows what a good layout looks like rather than stating a rule.

items.text: Reply with both complete files, then a list of the choices you made.
items.why: The shape of the answer, including an assumption list.

items.text: Return the level as JSON with a roofs list and a lamps list.
items.why: Structured output is a format request.

interactives.title: Rescuing a real request: the timer display
interactives.intro: A reader sent a coding agent this request for Lamplighter: “add a timer to the screen and make it look nice.” The agent drew small white numbers in the middle of the top edge, which vanished against the pale dusk sky. Improve the request one step at a time; think before revealing each answer.

steps.q: What did the original request leave undecided?
steps.a: Position and size, the time format (seconds or minutes and seconds), font and color, contrast against the background, what happens as time runs low, and what “nice” means. The agent chose a default for every one, and the contrast default failed.

steps.q: Turn the most important gaps into acceptance criteria.
steps.a: “The timer sits in the top-right corner, 16 px from both edges. It shows remaining time as m:ss. Its text meets the WCAG 2.2 contrast minimum of 4.5:1 against what is behind it (a dark panel behind the text is fine). In the last 10 seconds the text turns red.” Each line can now pass or fail.

steps.q: What output format and fence should the request include?
steps.a: “Change only the HUD drawing code in game.js. Reply with each changed function in full and say where it goes, then list any choices this request did not settle.” This keeps the agent away from gameplay code and surfaces its defaults.

steps.q: The new build puts the timer on top of the lamp counter, which was also in the top-right. Write the revision.
steps.a: “The timer now overlaps the lamp counter in the top-right. Move the lamp counter to the top-left, 16 px from both edges, with the same panel style. No HUD element may overlap another. Change only HUD layout code and recheck the four timer criteria.” The new rule about overlap becomes a permanent criterion in the spec.

interactives.title: The revision loop, in order
interactives.intro: Put the steps of a disciplined revision in order, starting from the moment the AI hands back its first result.
steps: Run or open the result and check each acceptance criterion
Write down which criteria fail, with evidence such as a measurement or a screenshot
Write a revision request naming the failure, the change and what must stay the same
Check the new result against every criterion, not only the ones you fixed
Update the written spec with anything you added or changed your mind about
interactives.explain: Checking comes before revising, because a revision without a named failure is just a second draw. Rechecking every criterion catches regressions, and updating the spec last keeps one written record of what you want instead of scattered chat messages.

slides.title: Chapter 1: How to Ask Exactly
bullets: Why vague prompts fail
The anatomy of a spec
Acceptance criteria and examples
Output format and the first revision
slides.notes: This chapter gives you the habits every later chapter builds on. Each craft chapter adds vocabulary, but you will always put it into the same six-part spec and check it the same way.

slides.title: A spec that nobody checked
bullets: Mars Climate Orbiter, lost September 23, 1999
Spec required newton-seconds; the file gave pound-force seconds
Effect of thruster firings underestimated by a factor of 4.45
The spec was right; no step checked the file against it
slides.notes: The lesson is not that the spec was bad. A correct spec still fails if no one verifies the delivered work against it, which is why criteria come with every request.

slides.title: Underspecification and defaults
bullets: A vague request fits many outputs
The model fills each gap with a typical default
Result: competent, generic work
Fix: answer each open question or delegate it explicitly
slides.notes: Use the golden rule from Anthropic’s guide: if a colleague with little context could not follow your prompt, neither can the model. List the stranger’s questions before sending.

slides.title: Ambiguity
bullets: Words with several readings: lighter, faster, fix it
Models usually pick one reading silently
AmbiEnt: GPT-4’s disambiguations correct 32% of the time vs 90% for the dataset’s
Name the thing and the quantity
slides.notes: Ambiguity is different from missing information: the words are there but point several ways. Replace them with the specific property and amount you mean.

slides.title: The six-part spec
bullets: Goal (with the reason)
Context
Constraints and non-goals
Acceptance criteria
Examples
Output format
slides.notes: Each part prevents one failure. Requirements engineering’s standard asks that each requirement be unambiguous, singular and verifiable, and those three tests apply to every line of a prompt.

slides.title: Goals, context and constraints
bullets: Give the reason: it lets the model generalize
Context: skill, platform, files, audience
Hard versus soft constraints
Non-goals stop scope creep
slides.notes: Anthropic’s example swaps “NEVER use ellipses” for the reason (a text-to-speech engine cannot pronounce them). A reason does more work than capital letters.

slides.title: Acceptance criteria
bullets: Pass or fail, same answer for anyone
Translate adjectives into measures
WCAG 2.2: 4.5:1 contrast for normal text
Given / When / Then for behavior
slides.notes: Criteria turn review from an impression into a checklist. Scenarios also make you think about edge cases, where most bugs live.

slides.title: Examples
bullets: Few-shot: a few worked examples in the prompt
Three to five, relevant and diverse, in tags
Examples teach shape, and their accidents
Label counterexamples clearly
slides.notes: Min and colleagues found demonstrations mainly convey format and the space of answers. Vary whatever you do not want copied.

slides.title: Output format
bullets: Ask for the form you will use
Structured output and JSON schemas for programs
Assumption lists expose hidden defaults
Clarifying questions for big, ambiguous tasks
slides.notes: Format decides how much work remains after the model finishes. As of October 2026, Anthropic’s API can enforce a JSON schema; in chat, a template does the job.

slides.title: The revision loop
bullets: Check every criterion first
Revise with failure, evidence, change and fence
Recheck everything to catch regressions
Update the spec, not only the chat
slides.notes: A bare “try again” adds no information. One change at a time, and no conclusions from a single run.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Every gap is a decision: make it or delegate it
Six parts: goal, context, constraints, criteria, examples, format
Make “done” checkable
Revise narrowly and keep the spec current
slides.notes: Your challenge is to rewrite three real prompts and write Lamplighter’s first spec. Chapter 2 explains the machinery behind defaults, randomness and context, so you can see why these habits work.

choices: A prompt that is too long for the context window
A request that fits many different outputs because it leaves decisions unstated
A model that has too few parameters
A word with two meanings
quiz.explanation: Underspecification means decisions were never stated, so many outputs fit. A word with two meanings is ambiguity, a related but different problem.

quiz.q: You ask, “Make the bats faster.” The agent doubles their wing-flap animation speed, but you meant flight speed. What went wrong?
choices: The model was not capable enough
The request needed a role
“Faster” was ambiguous, and the model picked one reading without saying so
The prompt was underspecified about the color of the bats
quiz.explanation: “Faster” could mean animation rate, flight speed or attack rate. Models usually choose one reading silently, which is why you name the property and the amount: “bats fly 20% faster.”

quiz.q: Which pair of requirement characteristics from ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 does this chapter treat as doing most of the work in prompts?
choices: Unambiguous and verifiable
Feasible and necessary
Complete and conforming
Singular and appropriate
quiz.explanation: Unambiguous means one reasonable reading, and verifiable means you can show it was met. Together they turn a wish into something a model can build and you can check.

quiz.q: A reader’s prompt to a coding agent says: “Make the HUD. Plain JavaScript. Two files max.” The agent spends its effort on an animated title screen. Which part of the spec was most clearly missing?
choices: Output format
Constraints
Examples
Goal, with the reason for the work
quiz.explanation: The constraints are present. What is missing is what the work is for and why, which would have told the agent to spend its effort on the HUD rather than on extras.

quiz.q: Which acceptance criterion best replaces “make the text readable”?
choices: “Text should be easy on the eyes.”
“Use a beautiful font.”
“All HUD text meets the WCAG 2.2 contrast minimum of 4.5:1 against its background.”
“Make sure players can read it.”
quiz.explanation: Only the third choice can be checked with a tool and gives the same answer to anyone who checks it. The others restate the wish.

quiz.q: According to Min and colleagues, what do demonstrations in a prompt mainly convey?
choices: The exact correct answer for each future input
The format, the kind of input and the set of possible answers
Nothing; examples have no measurable effect
The model’s training data
quiz.explanation: Replacing correct answers in examples with random ones hurt performance only slightly, which suggests examples mainly teach shape: format, input distribution and the space of possible answers.

quiz.q: Which revision request is best scoped?
choices: “It’s wrong, try again.”
“Redo the whole game but better.”
“Fix everything that seems off to you.”
“Criterion 2 fails: lamps light from about 64 px away. Make them light only on overlap. Change only the lamp check and list the lines you changed.”
quiz.explanation: The last choice names the failing criterion and evidence, states the change, fences the rest and asks for a list of changes. The others give the model no new information or invite unlimited changes.

quiz.q: After you fix the jump, the player starts falling through one roof that used to be solid. What is this called, and what habit would have caught it?
choices: A regression; rechecking every criterion after each revision
A hallucination; asking the model to be more careful
Underspecification; adding more adjectives
A default; regenerating the answer
quiz.explanation: A change that breaks something that used to work is a regression. Rechecking every criterion after each revision, not only the one you fixed, is how you catch it.

challenge.title: Three real prompts, rewritten
challenge.prompt: Find three prompts you actually sent to an AI tool in the last month, ideally one for code, one for an image and one for writing or design. For each, list the decisions it left to defaults and any ambiguous words. Rewrite each as a six-part spec, run both versions in the same tool, and compare the results against the acceptance criteria you wrote.
challenge.deliverable: For each of the three prompts: the original, the list of gaps, the rewritten spec, and four to six sentences comparing the two results criterion by criterion.
rubric: Gaps are named concretely and labeled as underspecified or ambiguous
Each rewrite contains all six parts, with at least two checkable acceptance criteria
Comparisons refer to the criteria, not just to overall impressions
At least one decision is delegated explicitly, with limits and a request to report the choice

challenge.title: Lamplighter spec v0.1 and its first revision
challenge.prompt: Write the complete spec for the first playable build of Lamplighter, using this chapter’s six parts, at least four acceptance criteria (two of them Given/When/Then scenarios with edge cases) and a text sketch of the level. Give it to a coding agent or chat assistant, run the result, check every criterion, and write one scoped revision request.
challenge.deliverable: The spec (no more than one page), a pass or fail table for every criterion with evidence, the assumption list the model returned, and your revision request.
rubric: The goal includes its reason, and the constraints include at least one non-goal
Every acceptance criterion is verifiable by someone else
The check table gives evidence (a measurement, a description of what happened) for each result
The revision names the failure, the change and the fence, and asks for all criteria to be rechecked
